steps.title: This is the board.
steps.body: 64 squares, light and dark, like a little town. Every game happens here.

steps.title: Files and ranks.
steps.body: Columns are files, named a to h. Rows are ranks, numbered 1 to 8. Here's the e-file and the 4th rank.

steps.title: Every square has a name.
steps.body: File first, then rank. Tap e4.
steps.hint: Find the e-file, then count up to rank 4.

steps.title: One more.
steps.body: Tap d5.
steps.hint: d is just left of e. Count up to 5.

steps.title: Light on the right.
steps.body: The square in your bottom-right corner is always light. Tap it.
steps.hint: Look at the corner nearest your right hand.

steps.title: Here's how a game starts.
steps.body: White sits at the bottom, Black at the top. Pawns stand in front; the big pieces wait behind them.

steps.title: Find the king.
steps.body: The king is the tallest piece, with a little cross. Tap the white king.
steps.hint: It's in the middle of the bottom row, on e1.

steps.title: The queen loves her colour.
steps.body: The white queen starts on a light square, right next to her king. Tap her.
steps.hint: She wears the spiky crown, on d1.

steps.title: Quick check.
steps.body: How many squares are on a chessboard?
steps.hint: 8 files times 8 ranks.

steps.title: The rook goes straight.
steps.body: Up, down, left or right, as far as it likes, until something is in the way.

steps.title: Collect the stars.
steps.body: Tap the rook, then tap where it should go. Visit every star.
steps.hint: Straight lines only. Go up to a5 first.

steps.title: The bishop slides diagonally.
steps.body: It stays on its own colour for the whole game.

steps.title: Diagonal stars.
steps.body: Guide the bishop to every star.
steps.hint: Corner to corner, like an X. e3 is two steps up and right.

steps.title: The queen does both.
steps.body: Straight like a rook, diagonal like a bishop. She's your strongest piece.

steps.title: Queen's tour.
steps.body: Visit all three stars with the queen.
steps.hint: Go straight up to d6, then think diagonally.

steps.title: The knight jumps.
steps.body: Two squares one way, then one to the side: an L. It's the only piece that hops over others.

steps.title: Hop, hop, hop.
steps.body: Jump the knight to each star.
steps.hint: From b1, two up and one right lands on c3.

steps.title: The king takes small steps.
steps.body: One square in any direction. Slow, but the most important piece you have.

steps.title: Little steps.
steps.body: Walk the king to both stars.
steps.hint: One diagonal step at a time.

steps.title: Quick check.
steps.body: Which piece can jump over other pieces?
steps.hint: Think of the L-shaped hop.

steps.title: Pawns march forward.
steps.body: One square at a time. On its very first move, a pawn may take two.

steps.title: A big first step.
steps.body: Move the pawn two squares forward.
steps.hint: Tap the pawn, then the square two above it.

steps.title: Pawns capture diagonally.
steps.body: A pawn can't take what's in front of it. It captures one square diagonally forward.

steps.title: Your turn to capture.
steps.body: Take the black pawn.
steps.hint: Diagonal, up and to the left.

steps.title: Small piece, big dreams.
steps.body: A pawn that reaches the far side becomes a queen, or any piece you like.

steps.title: Make a queen.
steps.body: Push the pawn to the last row.
steps.hint: One more step forward.

steps.title: Quick check.
steps.body: How do pawns capture?
steps.hint: Remember the black pawn you just took.

steps.title: Check!
steps.body: When a king is attacked, it's in check. It must get out of danger on the very next move.

steps.title: Spot it.
steps.body: Is the black king in check?
steps.hint: Follow the bishop's diagonal toward the king.

steps.title: Give check.
steps.body: Move your rook so it attacks the black king.
steps.hint: The king sits on the top row. Can your rook get there?

steps.title: Checkmate wins the game.
steps.body: Checkmate means the king is in check and has no way out. Here, the pawns block their own king.

steps.title: Checkmate in one.
steps.body: Find the move that traps the black king.
steps.hint: The king is stuck behind its pawns. Look at the top row.

steps.title: One more.
steps.body: Your queen and king work together. Checkmate!
steps.hint: Put the queen right next to the black king, where your king protects her.

steps.title: Check or checkmate?
steps.body: Black to move. What is this?
steps.hint: Can the king move, block or capture?

steps.title: Time for a real game.
steps.body: You play White, I play Black. I'll go gently. There's no clock, so take your time.

steps.title: A few good habits.
steps.body: Move a centre pawn, bring out knights and bishops, and keep your king safe. Have fun!

steps.title: Your first game
steps.body: You're White. Make your move.

steps.title: Castling.
steps.body: A special move: the king steps two squares toward a rook, and the rook hops over to its other side. It tucks your king away safely.

steps.title: Castle short.
steps.body: Tap the king, then the square two to its right.
steps.hint: The king goes to g1; the rook jumps to f1 by itself.

steps.title: Three rules.
steps.body: You can't castle out of check, through an attacked square, or after the king or that rook has moved.

steps.title: Spot it.
steps.body: Can White castle short here?
steps.hint: Follow the bishop's diagonal. Which square does it watch?

steps.title: Castle long.
steps.body: Now castle toward the queen's side.
steps.hint: Two squares to the left: c1.

steps.title: Why castle early?
steps.body: What does castling do for you?

options.label: Keeps the king safe and brings a rook out

steps.hint: Look where the king and rook ended up.

steps.title: En passant.
steps.body: If a pawn rushes two squares and lands beside your pawn, you may capture it as if it moved one. Only on the very next move.

steps.title: Capture en passant.
steps.body: Black just played d7 to d5. Take it!
steps.hint: Your pawn moves diagonally to d6, behind the black pawn.

steps.title: Stalemate is a draw.
steps.body: If the side to move has no legal moves but is not in check, the game is a draw. Winning players must watch out for it.

steps.title: What happened?
steps.body: Black to move. What is this position?
steps.hint: Is the black king in check right now?

steps.title: Win, don't draw.
steps.body: Give checkmate, and avoid stalemate.
steps.hint: Check from the top row. Your king covers the escape squares.

steps.title: What pieces are worth.
steps.body: Pawn 1 · Knight 3 · Bishop 3 · Rook 5 · Queen 9. The king is priceless. Use these to decide trades.

steps.title: Quick check.
steps.body: Which is worth more?
steps.hint: Rook 5, knight 3.

steps.title: Take the big one.
steps.body: Your knight can capture two things. Take the most valuable.
steps.hint: A rook is worth 5, a pawn only 1.

steps.title: Only safe captures.
steps.body: One capture loses your queen. Find the safe one.
steps.hint: The d5 pawn is protected by c6. The knight isn't protected.

steps.title: Good trade?
steps.body: You give a bishop (3) to win a rook (5).
steps.hint: 5 minus 3.

steps.title: The fork.
steps.body: One piece attacks two at once. The opponent can only save one. Knights are famous for it.

steps.title: Fork the king and rook.
steps.body: Jump your knight to attack both.
steps.hint: Which square is a knight's jump from both a8 and e8?

steps.title: Pawns fork too.
steps.body: Push a pawn to attack two pieces.
steps.hint: A pawn on d4 attacks c5 and e5.

steps.title: Queen fork.
steps.body: Check the king and hit the knight at the same time.
steps.hint: From e6 the queen sees g8 and b6.

steps.title: Quick check.
steps.body: What is a fork?

options.label: One piece attacking two at once

steps.hint: Look at the knight on c7.

steps.title: The pin.
steps.body: A pinned piece can't move without exposing something more valuable behind it. Here the knight shields its king.

steps.title: Can it move?
steps.body: Black to move. Can the knight on c6 move?

options.label: No, it's pinned to the king

steps.hint: What would the bishop attack if the knight stepped away?

steps.title: Make a pin.
steps.body: Pin the knight to the king with your bishop.
steps.hint: Line up bishop, knight and king on one diagonal.

steps.title: Attack the pinned piece.
steps.body: It can't run. Hit it with a pawn.
steps.hint: One step forward attacks c6.

steps.title: Quick check.
steps.body: A piece pinned to its king…
steps.hint: Moving it would put its own king in check.

steps.title: The ladder.
steps.body: Two rooks take turns: one guards a row, the other checks on the next. The king is pushed up, rung by rung, to the edge.

steps.title: Climb the ladder.
steps.body: Check, then check again with the other rook, until it's mate.
steps.hint: Always check on the row in front of the king with the rook that isn't guarding.

steps.title: Quick check.
steps.body: Where does the ladder push the king?

options.label: To the edge of the board

steps.hint: Look where it got stuck.

steps.title: Queen and king.
steps.body: The queen boxes the king in, your king walks up to help, then the queen delivers mate right next to it.

steps.title: Finish it.
steps.body: Checkmate with the queen.
steps.hint: Check along the top row. Your king covers a7 and b7.

steps.title: Careful: stalemate!
steps.body: One tempting move is a draw. Find the mate.
steps.hint: Qc7 leaves Black no moves but no check. Check from c8 instead.

steps.title: Mate in two.
steps.body: Push the king to the corner, then mate.
steps.hint: Take away the second row first.

lessons.title: The centre
lessons.sub: Start where the pieces reach furthest

steps.title: The centre.
steps.body: The four squares in the middle — d4, d5, e4 and e5 — are the centre. Pieces there reach more of the board.

steps.title: Open in the middle.
steps.body: Move a centre pawn two squares.
steps.hint: The pawn in front of your king.

steps.title: Black answers.
steps.body: A good reply also claims the centre. Now both e-pawns stand in the middle.

steps.title: A second centre pawn.
steps.body: Bring the d-pawn up beside it.
steps.hint: The pawn next to the one you already moved.

steps.title: Quick check.
steps.body: Which first move fights for the centre?
steps.hint: Look at the four middle squares.

steps.title: Bring the pieces out.
steps.body: Knights and bishops want to leave home early. Knights are happiest on f3, c3, f6 and c6, aimed at the centre.

steps.title: Develop the knight.
steps.body: Jump the king's knight toward the centre.
steps.hint: Two squares up and one toward the middle.

steps.title: Then the bishop.
steps.body: The light-squared bishop can go to c4. From there it looks down the diagonal toward f7.

steps.title: Put the bishop out.
steps.body: Develop the bishop to c4.
steps.hint: A long diagonal, two squares left of the knight.

steps.title: Quick check.
steps.body: In the opening, what should you do first?
steps.hint: The pieces on the back row want a job.

steps.title: The Italian game.
steps.body: A calm way to start: pawn to e4, knight to f3, bishop to c4, then castle. You will play all four.

steps.title: Play the opening.
steps.body: e4, Nf3, Bc4, and castle short. Black answers in the centre.
steps.hint: Centre pawn, knight, bishop, then the king steps to g1.

steps.title: What does the bishop eye?
steps.body: Your bishop on c4 aims at one square in particular.
steps.hint: Follow the diagonal from c4 toward Black's king.

lessons.title: Leave the queen at home
lessons.sub: Don't lead with your strongest piece

steps.title: Leave the queen at home.
steps.body: She is your strongest piece, so beginners rush her out. The other side then gains time by attacking her.

steps.title: Second move.
steps.body: You played e4, and Black played e5. What next?
steps.hint: Develop a piece. Save the queen.

steps.title: She gets chased.
steps.body: The knight on f6 attacks the queen. You have to move her again, and your other pieces are still at home.

steps.title: Tuck her back.
steps.body: Move the queen to e2, out of danger.
steps.hint: Back toward your own side, on the e-file.

lessons.title: The f7 square
lessons.sub: Why the king's pawn is tender

steps.title: f7 is tender.
steps.body: Before castling, f2 and f7 are defended only by the king. A bishop on c4 and a queen on h5 both look at f7.

steps.title: The scholar's mate.
steps.body: Take on f7 with the queen. It is mate, because the bishop protects her.
steps.hint: The queen and the bishop meet on f7.

steps.title: Would you count on it?
steps.body: This mate only works if f7 is left bare. A careful opponent defends it and then chases your queen.
steps.hint: The Italian game attacks f7 without risking the queen.

lessons.title: Skewers
lessons.sub: Attack through a more valuable piece

steps.title: The skewer.
steps.body: A rook, bishop or queen attacks a valuable piece, and a lesser piece sits behind it on the same line. The front piece must move. Then you take what was hiding.

steps.title: Skewer king and queen.
steps.body: Check the king so the queen behind it is lost.
steps.hint: Up the e-file, stopping just in front of the king.

steps.title: Quick check.
steps.body: How is a skewer different from a pin?

options.label: The more valuable piece is in front
The pieces are not on a line

steps.hint: Here the king is in front and the queen is behind.

lessons.title: Discovered attacks
lessons.sub: Step aside and uncover a check

steps.title: A discovered attack.
steps.body: One piece steps aside and uncovers an attack from the piece behind it. If that attack is a check, it is a discovered check.

steps.title: Step aside and take.
steps.body: Move the bishop, uncover the rook's check, and capture the queen.
steps.hint: The bishop leaves the e-file and lands on the queen.

steps.title: Quick check.
steps.body: Why is the queen lost?

options.label: The rook check means she cannot be saved
Bishops are worth more than queens

steps.hint: Black must answer the check from the rook.

lessons.title: Remove the guard
lessons.sub: Take the piece that protects another

steps.title: Remove the guard.
steps.body: The knight on c6 is the only piece defending the queen. Capture the guard, and the queen is loose.

steps.title: Take the knight.
steps.body: Capture the piece that guards the queen.
steps.hint: The bishop on b5 reaches the knight in one step.

steps.title: Now the queen.
steps.body: Nothing defends her. Take the queen.
steps.hint: Straight up the open file.

steps.title: Quick check.
steps.body: Before you capture a guarded piece, you can…
steps.hint: Think about the knight you just removed.

lessons.title: Double check
lessons.sub: Two checks, and the king must move

steps.title: Double check.
steps.body: Sometimes the piece that steps aside also gives check, and so does the piece it uncovers. Two checks at once. The king must move. It cannot capture one attacker and block the other.

steps.title: Check with both.
steps.body: Move the bishop so it checks, and the rook checks too.
steps.hint: A diagonal step that still attacks the king, off the e-file.

steps.title: Quick check.
steps.body: In a double check, Black can…
steps.hint: One move cannot answer two different checks.

lessons.title: The active king
lessons.sub: In the endgame the king fights

steps.title: The king joins in.
steps.body: While many pieces are on the board, the king hides. In the endgame it becomes a strong piece. Walk it toward the centre.

steps.title: Step up.
steps.body: Move your king toward the centre.
steps.hint: One square up and to the right.

steps.title: Quick check.
steps.body: In an endgame, the king should…
steps.hint: Few pieces are left to attack it.

steps.title: The opposition.
steps.body: When the kings face each other with one square between them, the side that does not have to move has the opposition. The other king must step aside.

steps.title: Take the opposition.
steps.body: Step straight toward the black king, leaving one square between you.
steps.hint: One square up the e-file.

steps.title: Who has it?
steps.body: The kings face each other. It is White to move.
steps.hint: The side that must move does not have the opposition.

lessons.title: Passed pawns
lessons.sub: A pawn with a clear road

steps.title: A passed pawn.
steps.body: A passed pawn has no enemy pawn on its file, or on the files beside it, that can block it or capture it. Its job is to march and become a queen.

steps.title: Start the march.
steps.body: Push the passed pawn.
steps.hint: Two squares on its first move.

steps.title: Quick check.
steps.body: A passed pawn is a pawn that…

options.label: No enemy pawn can stop it from the side
Sits on the edge of the board

steps.hint: Look at the e-file. Black has no pawns at all.

lessons.title: Escort the pawn
lessons.sub: Walk a pawn to a queen

steps.title: Walk with the pawn.
steps.body: A pawn on its own can be caught. The king walks beside it and keeps the enemy king away until the pawn promotes.

steps.title: Make a queen.
steps.body: Push the pawn. When the black king steps closer, promote.
steps.hint: One step, then the last step, and choose a queen.

steps.title: Quick check.
steps.body: Why does the king stand next to the pawn?

options.label: To keep the enemy king from taking it
The king has to promote too
Kings cannot move in an endgame

steps.hint: Look at how close the black king got.

lessons.title: Rook behind the pawn
lessons.sub: Help a passed pawn from behind

steps.title: Rook behind the pawn.
steps.body: The best square for a rook in a pawn ending is behind the passed pawn. The pawn moves up, and the rook keeps protecting it from behind.

steps.title: Get behind it.
steps.body: Move the rook to the file of the passed pawn, behind it.
steps.hint: Slide along the first rank to the e-file.

steps.title: Quick check.
steps.body: Where should the rook stand?
steps.hint: The pawn needs a clear road, with help from behind.

lessons.title: Back-rank mate
lessons.sub: When the king's own pawns trap it

steps.title: The back rank.
steps.body: Pawns on f7, g7 and h7 keep the king safe from the front, and they also trap it. A rook or queen on the 8th rank is mate.

steps.title: Mate on the 8th.
steps.body: Checkmate with the rook.
steps.hint: The whole top row is open. Go there.

steps.title: Why can't the king escape?
steps.body: Black to move would be lost. What holds the king in?

options.label: Its own pawns, and the rook on the 8th
The king is not in check

steps.hint: Look at f7, g7 and h7.

lessons.title: Smothered mate
lessons.sub: A knight mates a boxed-in king

steps.title: Smothered mate.
steps.body: A knight can mate a king that is boxed in by its own pieces. The king has no square, and it cannot capture a knight that jumps in from two squares away.

steps.title: Jump in.
steps.body: Checkmate with the knight.
steps.hint: The knight attacks h8 from f7.

steps.title: Quick check.
steps.body: Why is this mate only a knight's trick?

options.label: The king is smothered by its own rook and pawns
The knight is protected by a pawn
Kings cannot be mated in the corner

steps.hint: g8, g7 and h7 are all filled by Black's own pieces.

steps.title: Rook and knight.
steps.body: In the corner, a rook and a knight mate together. The rook checks on the h-file. The knight covers the escape square the rook cannot.

steps.title: The Arabian mate.
steps.body: Checkmate with the rook.
steps.hint: Up the h-file, next to the king. The knight already watches g8.

steps.title: Quick check.
steps.body: What does the knight do in this mate?

options.label: Covers the square the rook does not

steps.hint: Look at g8.

steps.title: Two bishops.
steps.body: Two bishops cover both colours. With your king beside them, they can drive the enemy king into a corner and mate.

steps.title: Mate with the bishops.
steps.body: Slide the bishop from b1 to e4.
steps.hint: The long diagonal from b1.

steps.title: Quick check.
steps.body: Why do you need both bishops?

options.label: Each bishop covers one colour of square
One bishop is enough for this mate

steps.hint: A single bishop never changes colour.

lessons.title: King and rook mate
lessons.sub: Cut the king off, then mate

steps.title: King and rook.
steps.body: The rook cuts the king off along a rank or file. Your king stands beside it and covers the squares the rook cannot. Then the rook mates on the edge.

steps.title: Mate on the edge.
steps.body: Checkmate with the rook.
steps.hint: The top row. Your king already covers the escape squares.

steps.title: One more.
steps.body: Same idea, other corner.
steps.hint: Use the top row again.

lessons.title: Sacrifices
lessons.sub: Give a piece up to open the king

steps.title: Give something up.
steps.body: A sacrifice is a move that loses material on purpose. You do it when the king is caught, or when you win more than you gave.

steps.title: The queen goes in.
steps.body: Put the queen on the back rank. The pawns block their own king.
steps.hint: Straight up to d8.

steps.title: Was it worth it?
steps.body: You gave nothing here, but the idea is the same. When is a sacrifice sound?

options.label: When it leads to mate or wins more than it cost
Whenever a piece can be taken
Only if you are already ahead

steps.hint: Count what you get back, not just what you lose.

steps.title: Pawns need neighbours.
steps.body: A pawn with a friend on the next file can be defended. A pawn standing alone is a target.

steps.title: Take the lonely pawn.
steps.body: The pawn on d5 has no pawn beside it. Capture it.
steps.hint: The knight jumps to d5.

steps.title: Quick check.
steps.body: Which pawn is easier to attack?

options.label: One in a chain of three

steps.hint: A neighbour can recapture.

lessons.title: Making a plan
lessons.sub: What to do when there is no tactic

steps.title: No tactic? Improve a piece.
steps.body: When nothing can be taken, don't push a random pawn. Bring a piece toward the centre.

steps.title: Develop the knight.
steps.body: Put the king's knight on f3.
steps.hint: Two up and one toward the centre.

steps.title: What is a plan?
steps.body: A plan is the next few moves with one aim.

options.label: Improve your pieces and keep the king safe
Move the same piece every turn
Trade everything as fast as you can

steps.hint: Think of the opening habits: centre, develop, castle.

lessons.title: Queen endings
lessons.sub: Win with a queen against a lone king

steps.title: Queen against a lone king.
steps.body: Use the queen to take a whole rank away, then walk your king up. Don't step so close that the king has no move and is not in check. That is stalemate.

steps.title: Mate on the edge.
steps.body: Check along the top rank.
steps.hint: The queen can reach h8 or b7.

steps.title: The trap.
steps.body: The king has no move, and it is not in check. What is that?
steps.hint: Look at the king's square. Is it attacked right now?

steps.title: The square of the pawn.
steps.body: Draw a square from the pawn to the promotion square, as wide as it is tall. If the defending king can step into that square, it can catch the pawn. If it cannot, the pawn runs home.

steps.title: The king is too far.
steps.body: Black's king is outside the square. Push the pawn.
steps.hint: Straight up the e-file.

steps.title: Quick check.
steps.body: When can a lone king stop a passed pawn?

options.label: When it can step into the pawn's square
Only if it stands in front of the pawn

steps.hint: Imagine the square to the promotion rank.

steps.title: Key squares.
steps.body: For a pawn to queen safely, your king must reach certain squares in front of it. For a pawn on e5, those key squares are d7, e7 and f7.

steps.title: Step toward a key square.
steps.body: Walk the king to f5, closer to f7.
steps.hint: One step up the f-file.

steps.title: Why they matter.
steps.body: What happens if your king reaches a key square?

options.label: The pawn can be escorted through
The pawn must be given up

steps.hint: The king clears a path and covers the promotion square.

steps.title: Rook pawns are different.
steps.body: A pawn on the a- or h-file is easier to draw against. If the defending king reaches the promotion corner, you usually cannot budge it without stalemate.

steps.title: The corner.
steps.body: Black's king has reached the promotion corner against a rook pawn. What is the usual result?
steps.hint: The king cannot be forced out without leaving it no legal move.

steps.title: A centre pawn is different.
steps.body: With a centre pawn and your king in front, you can still win. Push the pawn one step.

steps.title: Advance the pawn.
steps.body: Play e6, keeping the black king boxed.
steps.hint: One step up, next to their king.

steps.title: Lose a move on purpose.
steps.body: Sometimes the opposition works against you if it is your turn. You walk your king in a little triangle — three steps that end on the same square — so that it becomes their turn instead.

steps.title: Start the triangle.
steps.body: Step to e3 or c3. You are not running away — you are waiting.
steps.hint: One step to the right.

steps.title: What is the point?
steps.body: Why would you walk in a triangle?

options.label: To pass the move and gain the opposition
To hide the king in the corner

steps.hint: You want it to be their turn when the kings face each other.

lessons.title: Breakthrough
lessons.sub: Sacrifice a pawn to queen another

steps.title: Breakthrough.
steps.body: Three pawns facing three can still make a queen. The trick is to sacrifice one so another runs through.

steps.title: The break.
steps.body: Push the middle pawn to b6. Whatever Black takes with, a second pawn will get through.
steps.hint: The b-pawn, one step forward.

steps.title: Why it works.
steps.body: After b6, if Black takes with the a-pawn, what do you do?

options.label: Push c6, then the a-pawn will run

steps.hint: Keep sacrificing to clear a path on the other wing.

lessons.title: The Lucena position
lessons.sub: Build a bridge for the pawn

steps.title: The Lucena position.
steps.body: Your pawn is on the seventh, your king in front of it, and their king is cut off. The winning idea is a bridge: the rook checks their king away, then blocks a check so your king can come out and the pawn can queen.

steps.title: The end of the idea.
steps.body: The king and pawn already cover the escapes. Mate with the rook.
steps.hint: The rook can reach the back rank, on c8.

steps.title: The bridge.
steps.body: What is the rook's job in the Lucena?

options.label: Check the king away, then block a check so your king can leave
Give itself up for the pawn
Stay on the back rank forever

steps.hint: The rook both attacks and shields.

lessons.title: The Philidor defence
lessons.sub: Hold the third rank to draw

steps.title: The Philidor defence.
steps.body: When you are the one defending a rook ending, put your rook on the third rank (the sixth for them) and keep it there. Their king cannot come forward. When the pawn finally reaches the third, you check from behind.

steps.title: Hold the third rank.
steps.body: Park the rook on a3.
steps.hint: One step up the a-file.

steps.title: Then what?
steps.body: When their pawn reaches your third rank, what should the rook do?

options.label: Check the king from behind, on the file
Take the pawn at once, even if it hangs the rook
Move the king in front of the pawn

steps.hint: The king has no pawn shield once the pawn has stepped forward.

lessons.title: Cut the king off
lessons.sub: A rook takes a whole line away

steps.title: Cut the king off.
steps.body: A rook on a file or rank the enemy king cannot cross is worth a lot. The king is trapped on a short side of the board and cannot help its pawns.

steps.title: Cut the seventh.
steps.body: Slide the rook to d7. The king is now stuck on the last rank as well.
steps.hint: Straight up the d-file, just in front of their king.

steps.title: Quick check.
steps.body: A king that is cut off cannot…

options.label: Cross the rook's file or rank

steps.hint: The rook takes a whole line away.

lessons.title: Rook against a pawn
lessons.sub: Get behind it, then take it

steps.title: Rook against a pawn.
steps.body: A rook beats a pawn if you can get behind it, or check the king away, and then take it. Don't snatch a protected pawn if the king recaptures the rook — that is a draw.

steps.title: Take the unprotected pawn.
steps.body: The king is on c3, two squares away. The pawn on a2 is free.
steps.hint: The rook takes on a2.

steps.title: The trap.
steps.body: If the pawn is protected by the king, should you take it with the rook?

options.label: No — the king takes back and it is a draw

steps.hint: King and rook versus a lone king is a win. King versus king is a draw.

lessons.title: An active rook
lessons.sub: The seventh rank and behind pawns

steps.title: An active rook.
steps.body: In a rook ending, activity matters more than a pawn. A rook on the seventh rank attacks pawns from behind and can trap the king on the edge.

steps.title: To the seventh.
steps.body: Put the rook on a7.
steps.hint: Straight up the a-file, onto their second rank.

steps.title: Where does an active rook belong?
steps.body: Pick the best home.

options.label: Behind a passed pawn, or on the seventh rank
In front of its own pawns, blocking them

steps.hint: The rook wants open lines and weak pawns to chew.

steps.title: Overload.
steps.body: A piece with two jobs cannot do both at once. Here the black rook must guard the back rank and meet a check. Give the check, and the rank falls.

steps.title: Two jobs, one rook.
steps.body: Check on e8. When the rook takes, your queen recaptures and mates.
steps.hint: The e-file is open. Start with the rook.

steps.title: The idea.
steps.body: A piece is overloaded when…

options.label: It has to defend two things at once
It is worth more than a queen

steps.hint: Pull it away from one job, and the other collapses.

steps.title: Deflection.
steps.body: You pull a defender off a key square with a forcing move, then take what it left behind.

steps.title: Pull the queen away.
steps.body: Check on e8. The queen must take, and your queen mates on e8.
steps.hint: Check first, then recapture with the queen.

steps.title: Quick check.
steps.body: Deflection means…

options.label: Luring a defender off a square you want
Moving your king to the corner

steps.hint: You make the guard leave its post.

steps.title: Interference.
steps.body: Black's bishop on b7 defends the rook on e4, along the long diagonal. Drop a piece in the middle of that line, and the rook is suddenly hanging.

steps.title: Block the diagonal.
steps.body: Jump the knight to d5, right between the bishop and the rook.
steps.hint: The knight on c3 can land on d5.

steps.title: The idea.
steps.body: Interference works by…

options.label: Blocking the line between a piece and what it defends

steps.hint: A piece in the way means the defence no longer arrives.

steps.title: The in-between move.
steps.body: Don't recapture on instinct. A check in the middle of a sequence can change everything. Here the knight is hanging — but a rook check first wins the queen.

steps.title: Check first.
steps.body: Check on f7. When the king steps aside, take the queen.
steps.hint: The queen checks on f7, then the knight takes on c6.

steps.title: What is a zwischenzug?
steps.body: It's a German word players still use.

options.label: A useful move played in between, often a check

steps.hint: You insert a forcing move before you recapture.

lessons.title: Attraction
lessons.sub: Lure a piece onto a bad square

steps.title: Attraction.
steps.body: You lure a piece — often the king — onto a square where a tactic works. A queen check on g8 pulls the rook there, and the knight mates on f7.

steps.title: Pull the rook in.
steps.body: Check on g8. When the rook takes, mate with the knight.
steps.hint: The queen goes to g8, then the knight jumps to f7.

steps.title: The idea.
steps.body: Attraction means…

options.label: Forcing a piece onto a square where it can be punished

steps.hint: You invite them in, then strike.

steps.title: The windmill.
steps.body: A rook and a bishop work as a saw. The rook checks, the king hides, then the rook steps aside — a discovered check from the bishop — and swings back again, picking up pieces as it goes.

steps.title: Start the saw.
steps.body: Take on g7 with check. When the king goes to the corner, take on f7 with a discovered check.
steps.hint: The rook is already on the g-file. Take the g-pawn first.

steps.title: What makes it work?
steps.body: The discovered check comes from…

options.label: The bishop, once the rook steps off the diagonal

steps.hint: Look at the bishop on b2 and the long diagonal to h8.

steps.title: The Greek gift.
steps.body: A classic sacrifice: the bishop takes on h7, the knight hops to g5, and the queen comes to h5. You give a piece to rip the king's shield off.

steps.title: Play the sacrifice.
steps.body: Bishop takes h7, knight to g5, queen to h5.
steps.hint: Start with the bishop on d3. The h-pawn is the target.

steps.title: The point.
steps.body: Why give the bishop on h7?

options.label: To draw the king out and bring queen and knight in
To win a pawn and stop there

steps.hint: The follow-up is Ng5 and Qh5, not a quiet retreat.

steps.title: Opposite-side castling.
steps.body: When the kings live on opposite wings, the game becomes a race. You throw pawns at their king, and they throw pawns at yours. The first one to open a file usually wins.

steps.title: Start the race.
steps.body: Push the h-pawn two squares, toward their king.
steps.hint: The pawn in front of the h-rook.

steps.title: The plan.
steps.body: When the kings are on opposite sides, you should…

options.label: Storm pawns at their king and not delay
Trade all the pawns in the centre and stop
Hide every piece on the back rank

steps.hint: It is a race, not an ending.

steps.title: The pawn storm.
steps.body: Pawns are the cheapest way to open a king's files. Push them toward the shield, trade, and let the rooks and queen use the open lines.

steps.title: Cramp the shield.
steps.body: Push the h-pawn one more step, to h5.
steps.hint: The pawn already on h4 goes to h5.

steps.title: Then what?
steps.body: Once a file opens in front of their king, who should use it?

options.label: Your heavy pieces: rooks and the queen
You should close the file again

steps.hint: Open files belong to the big pieces.

lessons.title: The rook lift
lessons.sub: Swing a rook over on the third rank

steps.title: The rook lift.
steps.body: A rook does not have to stay on the back rank. You can lift it to the third rank and swing it across toward the enemy king.

steps.title: Swing the rook over.
steps.body: Lift the rook to a3, then swing it to g3.
steps.hint: Up to a3 first, then across the third rank.

steps.title: Why lift?
steps.body: A rook lift is useful because…

options.label: The rook joins the attack without waiting for an open file on the first rank
It hides the rook from the game
It is the only way to castle

steps.hint: The third rank is a road across the board.

lessons.title: Batteries
lessons.sub: Two pieces aiming the same way

steps.title: A battery.
steps.body: Two pieces aiming the same way — a bishop and a queen on a diagonal, or two rooks on a file — are a battery. The front piece can step aside or even be given up, and the back one still hits the target.

steps.title: Form the battery.
steps.body: Put the queen on c2, behind the bishop, aiming at h7.
steps.hint: One step left and up, onto c2.

steps.title: Quick check.
steps.body: In a battery, if the front piece is captured or moves…

options.label: The piece behind it still attacks the same target

steps.hint: They share one line.

lessons.title: The Queen's Gambit
lessons.sub: Offer a wing pawn for the centre

steps.title: The Queen's Gambit.
steps.body: A different way to start: the d-pawn first, then c4. You offer a wing pawn so you can fight for the centre. Black does not have to take it.

steps.title: Play the opening.
steps.body: d4, then c4, then develop the king's knight.
steps.hint: The d-pawn first, then the c-pawn, then the knight to f3.

steps.title: The offer.
steps.body: Why does White offer the c-pawn?

options.label: To trade a wing pawn for more control of the centre
To give Black a free queen

steps.hint: If Black takes on c4, White can build a big centre with e4 later.

lessons.title: The Sicilian idea
lessons.sub: Fight for d4 with a c-pawn

steps.title: The Sicilian idea.
steps.body: Against e4, Black can fight for the centre with a c-pawn: …c5. You will still play Nf3 and d4, and open the d-file.

steps.title: Meet the Sicilian.
steps.body: e4, knight to f3, then d4.
steps.hint: Centre pawn, knight, then the d-pawn two squares.

steps.title: Black's idea.
steps.body: What does …c5 fight for?

options.label: The d4 square, without blocking the c-file
A quick checkmate on move two

steps.hint: The c-pawn watches d4 from the side.

steps.title: A solid centre.
steps.body: Black can also meet e4 with …e6 (the French) or …c6 (the Caro-Kann), then …d5. The centre often locks. You push e5 and attack on a wing.

steps.title: The Advance.
steps.body: e4, d4, and when Black plays …d5, close the centre with e5.
steps.hint: Two centre pawns, then one more step to e5.

steps.title: A locked centre.
steps.body: When the centre pawns are locked, the plan is usually to…

options.label: Attack on a wing, because the centre cannot open easily

steps.hint: Locked pawns point to a side of the board.

lessons.title: Don't move the same piece twice

steps.title: Don't move the same piece twice.
steps.body: In the opening, every tempo matters. Bring a new piece out, or castle, before you go pawn-hunting with a piece that already has a job.

steps.title: Tuck the king away.
steps.body: Castle short rather than starting a new adventure with the knight.
steps.hint: The king steps two squares toward the rook.

steps.title: A good habit.
steps.body: In the opening, what should you usually avoid?

options.label: Moving the same piece again before the others are out

steps.hint: New pieces want a job too.

lessons.title: Look before you take
lessons.sub: Legal's mate, and how to avoid it

steps.title: Look before you take.
steps.body: Some traps look like a free queen. Legal's mate is the famous warning: if you snatch the queen and ignore a check, you can be mated in a few moves. You will play the winning side, so you see how it works — and how to avoid it.

steps.title: Legal's mate.
steps.body: Play the trap. After the bishop takes your queen, the bishop check and the knight mate finish it.
steps.hint: After the knights and bishop are out, take on e5. Leave the queen if they take it, and aim at f7.

steps.title: The lesson.
steps.body: Before you take a 'free' piece in the opening, you should…

options.label: Check whether you are walking into a mate or a fork
Always take it as fast as you can

steps.hint: Count the checks that come after the capture.

steps.title: A knight outpost.
steps.body: An outpost is a square in the opponent's half that a pawn cannot chase you from. A knight there is a pest for the rest of the game.

steps.title: Park the knight.
steps.body: Jump the knight to e4. The c- and e-pawns cannot kick it.
steps.hint: From c3, two up and one to the right.

steps.title: What makes an outpost?
steps.body: A good outpost is a square…

options.label: That enemy pawns cannot drive a piece off
That only a rook can stand on

steps.hint: Look at whether a pawn can ever attack that square.

lessons.title: Good bishop, bad bishop
lessons.sub: Don't let your pawns block you

steps.title: Good bishop, bad bishop.
steps.body: A bishop is unhappy when its own pawns sit on the same colour and block it. It is happy when those pawns are on the other colour, leaving its diagonals open.

steps.title: Get it outside the chain.
steps.body: Slide the bishop to a5, off the blocked squares.
steps.hint: A long diagonal to the left, up to a5.

steps.title: Quick check.
steps.body: A bishop is 'bad' when…

options.label: Its own pawns stand on the same colour and get in the way

steps.hint: The pawns and the bishop should not fight for the same squares.

steps.title: Space.
steps.body: Pawns that stand further up the board give your pieces more room and leave the opponent cramped. A space advantage is something you can slowly use, not a tactic you cash in one move.

steps.title: Take more space.
steps.body: Push the d-pawn to d5.
steps.hint: The pawn on d4 goes one step forward.

steps.title: What space does.
steps.body: A space advantage usually means…

options.label: Your pieces have more room; theirs feel cramped
You must checkmate on the next move

steps.hint: Think of how freely the pieces can move.

steps.title: When to trade.
steps.body: If you are ahead, trading pieces (not always pawns) makes the win simpler. Here you are a rook up. Offering a queen trade is a good practical choice.

steps.title: Trade queens.
steps.body: Take the queen on e6. Black can recapture, and you stay a rook up in a much simpler position.
steps.hint: Straight up the e-file.

steps.title: The rule of thumb.
steps.body: When you are ahead in material, it is usually good to…

options.label: Trade pieces and keep the extra material
Give the extra piece back at once

steps.hint: Fewer pieces means fewer surprises, and your extra one is felt more.

lessons.title: Stop their idea
lessons.sub: Prevent a plan before it starts

steps.title: Stop their idea.
steps.body: A good move is sometimes a quiet one that stops what they wanted to do. The knight on c6 would love to jump to b4 and attack the queen. A little pawn move takes that square away.

steps.title: Take the square away.
steps.body: Play a3, so the knight cannot land on b4.
steps.hint: The a-pawn, one step.

steps.title: Prophylaxis means…
steps.body: The word is used a lot in chess books.

options.label: Preventing the opponent's plan before it starts

steps.hint: Ask what they want, then see if a cheap move stops it.

steps.title: Convert an extra pawn.
steps.body: When you are a pawn up, the plan is usually: trade pieces, keep pawns, and use your king. Don't get so greedy that you allow a stalemate or a perpetual.

steps.title: Push the extra pawn.
steps.body: Play e7, driving the king back.
steps.hint: The pawn goes one step, next to their king.

steps.title: A practical rule.
steps.body: You are a pawn up in the ending. What should you usually do?

options.label: Trade pieces, keep pawns, and advance the extra one

steps.hint: Simplifying pieces makes the extra pawn easier to queen.

lessons.title: When to take a draw
lessons.sub: Perpetual check is a good save

steps.title: When to take a draw.
steps.body: If you are losing, a draw is a good save. A perpetual check — checking the king over and over so it cannot escape — is one way. Stalemate is another.

steps.title: Check, and check again.
steps.body: Check on f8, then on f7. The king is bouncing between two squares. That is how a perpetual starts.
steps.hint: The queen can check from f8 first.

steps.title: A good save.
steps.body: If you are otherwise losing, a perpetual check is…

options.label: A draw, and a good practical result
A win for the side being checked

steps.hint: The same checks can be repeated, and the game is drawn.

lessons.title: Stay calm in defence
lessons.sub: Take, block, or move the king

steps.title: Stay calm in defence.
steps.body: When you are in check or under threat, first make a list: can you take the attacker, can you block, or must the king move? Don't panic and give material away.

steps.title: Block the check.
steps.body: The queen on d1 is checking you. Interpose the rook on e1.
steps.hint: The rook can drop onto e1, between the queen and your king.

steps.title: Three ways out of check.
steps.body: When you are in check, you may…

options.label: Capture the attacker, block the line, or move the king

steps.hint: Those are the only three legal replies.

steps.title: Checks, captures, threats.
steps.body: When you calculate, start with forcing moves: checks first, then captures, then threats. A quiet-looking position can hide a check that wins at once.

steps.title: Look at the check first.
steps.body: Check on d8. The queen can block, but then you take it and mate.
steps.hint: The d-file is open, all the way to the back rank.

steps.title: Where do you start?
steps.body: Every time you calculate a position, look first at…
steps.hint: Forcing moves shrink the list you have to see.

lessons.title: Anastasia's mate
lessons.sub: Knight and rook on the edge

steps.title: Anastasia's mate.
steps.body: A knight on e7 guards g8 and g6. The king is stuck on the h-file behind its own pawn, so a rook down the h-file finishes it.

steps.title: Close the h-file.
steps.body: Swing the rook to the h-file for checkmate.
steps.hint: The rook on d1 can slide all the way to h1.

steps.title: The knight's job.
steps.body: In Anastasia's mate, what does the knight do?

options.label: Guards the squares the king would run to

steps.hint: Look at g8 and g6.

steps.title: Boden's mate.
steps.body: Two bishops on crossing diagonals. One covers b8 and c7, the other checks from a6. The king's own pieces block the rest.

steps.title: Cross the diagonals.
steps.body: Find the bishop move that checkmates.
steps.hint: The bishop on e2 has a long way to go: all the way to a6.

steps.title: Why it works.
steps.body: What makes Boden's mate possible?

options.label: A queen on the back rank
A pawn on the seventh rank

steps.hint: Count the bishops.

lessons.title: The kiss of death
lessons.sub: A guarded queen next to the king

steps.title: The kiss of death.
steps.body: A queen right next to the king, protected by another piece, is often mate. Here the bishop on b2 guards g7 from far away.

steps.title: Plant the queen.
steps.body: Put the queen next to the king where the bishop protects her.
steps.hint: Follow the long diagonal: d4, e5, f6, g7.

steps.title: Why can't the king take?
steps.body: After the queen lands on g7, why can't the king capture her?

options.label: The bishop on b2 protects her
The rook on e8 is in the way

steps.hint: Trace the diagonal from b2.

steps.title: The epaulette mate.
steps.body: When rooks stand on both sides of the king like shoulder pads, the king cannot step sideways. One check from the front can be mate.

steps.title: Check from the front.
steps.body: Find the queen move that checkmates.
steps.hint: From e6 the queen covers d7, e7 and f7 at once.

steps.title: Who traps the king?
steps.body: What stops the king from escaping sideways?

options.label: Its own rooks on d8 and f8

steps.hint: Look either side of the king.

steps.title: Damiano's mate.
steps.body: A pawn on g6 supports the queen on h7. The castled king is trapped by its own rook.

steps.title: Land on h7.
steps.body: Find checkmate.
steps.hint: Run the queen up the h-file.

steps.title: The pawn's job.
steps.body: What does the pawn on g6 do?
steps.hint: Which squares does a g6 pawn attack?

steps.title: Checkmate.
steps.body: Look for checks first. A checkmate is a check the king cannot escape: no safe square, no block, no capture. Each one takes a single move.

steps.title: Checkmate 1 of 5
steps.body: White to move. Checkmate in one move.
steps.hint: Start with your rook on b8.

steps.title: Checkmate 2 of 5
steps.body: White to move. Checkmate in one move.
steps.hint: Start with your queen on e4.

steps.title: Checkmate 3 of 5
steps.body: White to move. Checkmate in one move.
steps.hint: Start with your rook on f1.

steps.title: Checkmate 4 of 5
steps.body: White to move. Checkmate in one move.
steps.hint: Start with your queen on d4.

steps.title: Checkmate 5 of 5
steps.body: White to move. Checkmate in one move.
steps.hint: Start with your queen on a4.

steps.title: Forks.
steps.body: A fork attacks two things with one move. They can only save one of them, so you win the other. Some take more than one move: keep going after Black replies.

steps.title: Forks 1 of 5
steps.body: White to move. Attack two things at once. It takes 2 moves.
steps.hint: Start with your knight on c6. After Black replies, look for the follow-up.

steps.title: Forks 2 of 5
steps.body: White to move. Attack two things at once. It takes 2 moves.
steps.hint: Start with your knight on d4. After Black replies, look for the follow-up.

steps.title: Forks 3 of 5
steps.body: White to move. Attack two things at once. It takes 2 moves.
steps.hint: Start with your knight on d7. After Black replies, look for the follow-up.

steps.title: Forks 4 of 5
steps.body: White to move. Attack two things at once. It takes 2 moves.
steps.hint: Start with your knight on b7. After Black replies, look for the follow-up.

steps.title: Forks 5 of 5
steps.body: White to move. Attack two things at once. It takes 2 moves.
steps.hint: Start with your bishop on d5. After Black replies, look for the follow-up.

steps.title: Pins.
steps.body: A pinned piece cannot move without exposing something more valuable behind it. Attack it, or pin it yourself. Some take more than one move: keep going after Black replies.

steps.title: Pins 1 of 5
steps.body: White to move. Use the pin. It takes 2 moves.
steps.hint: Start with your rook on a8. After Black replies, look for the follow-up.

steps.title: Pins 2 of 5
steps.body: White to move. Use the pin. It takes 2 moves.
steps.hint: Start with your rook on a7. After Black replies, look for the follow-up.

steps.title: Pins 3 of 5
steps.body: White to move. Use the pin. It takes 2 moves.
steps.hint: Start with your rook on a6. After Black replies, look for the follow-up.

steps.title: Pins 4 of 5
steps.body: White to move. Use the pin. It takes 2 moves.
steps.hint: Start with your rook on b1. After Black replies, look for the follow-up.

steps.title: Pins 5 of 5
steps.body: White to move. Use the pin. It takes 2 moves.
